name: Agag
title: King of the Amalekites
summary: Agag was the ruler of the Amalekites at the time when God commanded King Saul to carry out judgment against this people. Despite God's explicit command for total destruction, Saul let Agag live—an act of disobedience that had far-reaching consequences. The prophet Samuel proclaimed that God had rejected Saul as king of Israel, and then executed Agag himself in Gilgal. The figure of Agag also carries a broader theological dimension: in the book of Esther, Haman is referred to as an "Agagite", possibly a descendant of the Amalekite royal line. This connection illustrates how the enmity of the Amalekites against God's people persisted through generations, and underscores the serious consequences of Saul's disobedience.

keyEvents.title: Balaam's prophecy about Agag
keyEvents.description: In Balaam's prophetic utterance, Agag (or an Amalekite royal title) is mentioned in connection with Israel's future greatness. It is prophesied that Israel's kingdom will be exalted above Agag, pointing forward to Israel's superiority over the Amalekites.

keyEvents.title: God's command to destroy the Amalekites
keyEvents.description: God commands King Saul through the prophet Samuel to attack the Amalekites and completely destroy everything they own, sparing no one or anything.

keyEvents.title: Saul defeats the Amalekites but spares Agag
keyEvents.description: Saul defeated the Amalekites in battle, but instead of obeying God's command, he spared King Agag's life and kept the best of the livestock.

keyEvents.title: Samuel confronts Saul with his disobedience
keyEvents.description: The prophet Samuel confronts Saul with his disobedience to God's command. Samuel declares that obedience is better than sacrifice, and that God has rejected Saul as king over Israel.

keyEvents.title: Samuel Kills Agag
keyEvents.description: Samuel orders that Agag be brought before him. Agag approaches Samuel—how he behaved in this moment is debated—and appears to expect the worst is over. However, Samuel declares judgment upon him and cuts him down before the Lord in Gilgal.

keyEvents.title: Haman as a Descendant of Agag
keyEvents.description: In the Book of Esther, Haman is identified as an Agagite, a possible descendant of Agag and the Amalekites, who planned to exterminate the Jews in the Persian Empire.

versions.summary: Agag was the king of the Amalekites who was defeated by King Saul in battle. Saul spared Agag's life against God's command to completely destroy the Amalekites, which led to God rejecting Saul as king over Israel. Agag was eventually killed by the prophet Samuel in Gilgal.

footnotes.text: The name 'Agag' may have been a dynastic title for the kings of the Amalekites, just as 'Pharaoh' was a title for Egypt's rulers. This is supported by Balaam mentioning 'Agag' in his prophecy (Num 24:7) several generations before Saul's time, suggesting it could refer to another king or a general title.

The Hebrew word 'herem' (חֵרֶם), used for the command in 1 Sam 15, means total banishment or consecration to destruction. This was a form of holy war where everything—people, animals, and property—was to be destroyed as an offering to God. The concept has parallels in other ancient Near Eastern cultures, including the Mesha Stele from Moab.

The connection between Agag and Haman 'the Agagite' in the Book of Esther (Est 3:1) has been the subject of much rabbinic discussion. Rabbinic tradition (including Targum Sheni and the Talmud, Megillah 13a) claims that Haman was a direct descendant of Agag, and that Saul's failure to kill Agag allowed this hostile lineage to survive—nearly leading to the extermination of the Jews in Persia.

The Hebrew word 'ma'adannot' (מַעֲדַנֹּת) in 1 Sam 15:32, describing how Agag came before Samuel, is highly debated. Various translations render it as 'hesitantly', 'with cautious steps', 'in chains', or 'confidently'. The exact meaning of the word is uncertain and affects how one understands Agag's state of mind in his final moments.

The Amalekites were a nomadic people in the Negev Desert and the Sinai Peninsula. They attacked Israel right after the Exodus from Egypt (Exod 17:8-16), and this attack—directed at the weakest stragglers at the rear of the group (Deut 25:17-18)—is the background for God's command to destroy them. Archaeologically, the Amalekites are difficult to identify, as nomadic peoples leave few traces.

Saul's disobedience in connection with the Agag episode marks a turning point in Israel's monarchical history. God's rejection of Saul as king (1 Sam 15:23) paves the way for David's anointing and rise, and the event becomes a paradigmatic example that obedience to God is valued over outward religious acts.
